1.summary: Paul greets the Roman believers, longs to visit them, declares he is not ashamed of the gospel, and describes how humanity, knowing God through creation, refused to honor him and was handed over to its own desires.
1.lookfor: Notice the theme statement in verses 16 and 17, and the repeated phrase that God gave them up.

names.name: Paul
names.gloss: The apostle to the Gentiles, writing before his first visit to Rome.

names.name: Rome
names.gloss: The capital of the empire, with a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles.

names.name: David
names.gloss: Israel's great king, from whose line the Messiah came.

insights.title: A church Paul didn't found
insights.body: Paul hadn't founded or visited the Roman church (1:13). It likely began with Jews from Rome who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost. He writes partly to introduce himself.

insights.title: The theme
insights.body: Paul is not ashamed of the good news: it is God's power for salvation for everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, because in it God's righteousness is revealed (1:16-17). The rest of the letter unpacks these two verses.

insights.title: The righteous shall live by faith
insights.body: Paul quotes Habakkuk: the righteous shall live by faith (1:17). The verse later sparked Martin Luther's rediscovery of grace at the start of the Reformation.

insights.title: The righteousness of God
insights.body: The righteousness of God (1:17) means both God's own faithfulness to do right and keep his promises, and the right standing he gives to those who trust him.

insights.title: Without excuse
insights.body: God's eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen in what he has made, so people are without excuse (1:20). The problem isn't lack of evidence but refusal to give thanks.

insights.title: God gave them up
insights.body: Three times Paul says God gave them up (1:24, 1:26, 1:28). God's wrath here is not sudden lightning but letting people have what they insist on, and its consequences.

insights.title: Thankfulness
insights.body: The slide begins when people knew God but didn't glorify him or give thanks (1:21). What would more thankfulness change in you today?

2.summary: Paul turns to those who judge others, warning that God judges everyone impartially by their deeds; having the law or circumcision doesn't protect anyone who doesn't keep it, for a true Jew is one inwardly.
2.lookfor: Notice who Paul is addressing now, and his surprising definition of a true Jew.

names.name: Jew
names.gloss: A member of God's covenant people Israel.

names.name: Greek
names.gloss: Paul's shorthand for non-Jews, Gentiles.

insights.title: The moralist
insights.body: Having described pagan sin, Paul turns on the reader who has been nodding along: you who judge do the same things (2:1). No one gets to sit in the judge's seat.

insights.title: Kindness leads to repentance
insights.body: God's goodness is meant to lead you to repentance (2:4). His patience is not approval but an invitation.

insights.title: No partiality
insights.body: There is no partiality with God (2:11). Jew and Greek face the same standard; privilege doesn't purchase exemption.

insights.title: The law written on hearts
insights.body: Gentiles who don't have the law sometimes do by nature what it requires, showing its work written on their hearts and their consciences bearing witness (2:14-15). Conscience is a universal, imperfect witness.

insights.title: Circumcision of the heart
insights.body: True circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (2:29). Moses and Jeremiah had already called Israel to circumcise their hearts.

insights.title: Blasphemed among the nations
insights.body: Paul quotes Isaiah: God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you (2:24). Israel was meant to be a light to the nations; failing the law dims that light.

insights.title: Judging
insights.body: It's easy to condemn in others what we excuse in ourselves. Where are you quickest to judge?

3.summary: Paul answers objections about God's faithfulness, concludes that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin, and announces that God's righteousness has now been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus, whose death was a sacrifice of atonement.
3.lookfor: Notice the chain of Old Testament quotes in verses 10 to 18, and the turning point at "but now" in verse 21.

names.name: Jews
names.gloss: God's covenant people, entrusted with his words.

names.name: Gentiles
names.gloss: All the nations other than Israel.

insights.title: Entrusted with God's words
insights.body: The advantage of being Jewish is great: they were entrusted with the oracles of God (3:2). Paul never dismisses Israel's privilege, even while showing it can't save.

insights.title: No one righteous
insights.body: Paul strings together verses from the Psalms and Isaiah: there is no one righteous, no not one (3:10-18). The quotations move from heart to throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet and eyes, covering the whole person.

insights.title: But now
insights.body: After three chapters of bad news, Paul turns: but now, apart from the law, God's righteousness has been revealed (3:21). Some call these the two most important words in the letter.

insights.title: Justified
insights.body: Justified (3:24) is a law-court word: declared in the right. It's freely given by grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, the price paid to free a slave.

insights.title: Propitiation
insights.body: God set forth Jesus as an atoning sacrifice, or mercy seat (3:25). The Greek word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

insights.title: Just and justifier
insights.body: Why the cross? So that God might be just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus (3:26). He neither ignores sin nor condemns the sinner who trusts him.

insights.title: All have sinned
insights.body: All have sinned and fall short of God's glory (3:23), the same ground for everyone. How does that change the way you see the people around you?

4.summary: Paul shows from Scripture that Abraham was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised, making him the father of all who believe; his faith trusted God's promise against all odds, and the same righteousness is counted to us who believe in Jesus' resurrection.
4.lookfor: Notice the word "counted" or "credited" repeated through the chapter, and the timing of Abraham's circumcision.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: The father of Israel, called to trust God's promise of countless descendants.

names.name: David
names.gloss: The king who wrote of the blessing of forgiven sin.

names.name: Sarah
names.gloss: Abraham's wife, who bore Isaac in old age.

insights.title: Abraham believed God
insights.body: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (4:3), quoting Genesis 15. Paul's whole argument hangs on that verse.

insights.title: Counted
insights.body: The word for counted or credited, logizomai, appears eleven times in this chapter. It's an accounting term: entered on the books in someone's favor.

insights.title: Blessed is the one
insights.body: Paul adds David's words from Psalm 32: blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven (4:7-8). Two witnesses, Abraham and David, testify to righteousness as a gift.

insights.title: Before circumcision
insights.body: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, years before he was circumcised in Genesis 17 (4:10). So he is father of uncircumcised believers as well as circumcised ones.

insights.title: Hoping against hope
insights.body: Abraham, about a hundred years old, with Sarah's womb as good as dead, hoped against hope and grew strong in faith (4:18-20). Faith doesn't deny the facts; it trusts God beyond them.

insights.title: Calls things that are not
insights.body: Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were (4:17). The same God raised Jesus, and it's in him that we believe (4:24).

insights.title: Promises against the odds
insights.body: Abraham faced his limits honestly and still trusted. What fact in your life makes trusting God hard right now?

5.summary: Justified by faith, we have peace with God and hope that does not disappoint, because God showed his love by Christ dying for us while we were sinners; as sin and death came through Adam, grace and life overflow through Christ.
5.lookfor: Notice the chain from suffering to hope in verses 3 to 5, and the comparison between Adam and Christ.

names.name: Adam
names.gloss: The first man, through whom sin entered the world.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The giver of the law.

insights.title: Peace with God
insights.body: Being justified by faith, we have peace with God (5:1). Not just a feeling of peace, but the end of hostility: enemies have become friends.

insights.title: Suffering to hope
insights.body: Suffering works perseverance; perseverance, proven character; character, hope (5:3-4). And hope doesn't disappoint, because God's love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit (5:5).

insights.title: While we were still sinners
insights.body: God commends his own love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (5:8). Love doesn't wait for us to deserve it.

insights.title: Two men
insights.body: Through one man, Adam, sin and death entered the world; through one man, Jesus Christ, grace and life overflow (5:12-19). Humanity is gathered under two heads.

insights.title: Much more
insights.body: Paul repeats much more again and again (5:9, 5:10, 5:15, 5:17). Christ doesn't merely undo Adam's damage; grace outweighs it.

insights.title: Why the law came in
insights.body: The law came in so that the trespass would abound, but where sin abounded, grace abounded more (5:20). The law exposed the disease; it couldn't cure it.

insights.title: Loved first
insights.body: Christ died for you before you had done anything good. How does it feel to be loved without having earned it?

6.summary: Paul answers whether we should keep sinning so grace may increase: no, for in baptism we died with Christ and rose to new life; so don't let sin reign, but offer yourselves to God, since sin's wages are death but God's gift is eternal life.
6.lookfor: Notice the question that opens the chapter, the picture of baptism, and the contrast between wages and gift.

insights.title: Shall we continue in sin?
insights.body: If grace grows where sin grows, should we keep sinning? May it never be! (6:1-2). Paul's grace was so radical that people accused him of permitting sin.

insights.title: Buried and raised
insights.body: In baptism believers are buried with Christ into death so that, as he was raised, they may walk in newness of life (6:4). Going under the water and coming up enacts death and resurrection.

insights.title: Reckon
insights.body: Consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God (6:11). The word is the same accounting word as in chapter 4: count it as true, because it is.

insights.title: Instruments
insights.body: Don't present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but to God (6:13). The word can mean tools or weapons: your body is used for one side or the other.

insights.title: Slaves
insights.body: Slavery was everywhere in Rome, and perhaps a third of the city's people were slaves. Paul uses the familiar image: you are slaves of whatever you obey, either sin or righteousness (6:16).

insights.title: Wages and gift
insights.body: The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (6:23). Death is earned; life can only be received.

insights.title: Who's the master?
insights.body: Paul says we always serve something. What habit or desire has been acting like your master lately?

7.summary: Paul explains that believers have died to the law, which is holy but which sin used to produce death; he describes the struggle of wanting to do good but doing evil, crying out who will rescue me, and answering with thanks through Jesus Christ.
7.lookfor: Notice the marriage illustration, Paul's defense of the law as good, and the famous struggle in verses 14 to 25.

insights.title: The marriage picture
insights.body: A wife is bound to her husband while he lives, but free if he dies (7:2-3). Through Christ's body we died to the law and now belong to another, the risen Christ.

insights.title: Is the law sin?
insights.body: No, the law is holy, and the commandment holy, righteous and good (7:12). Sin used the commandment as a beachhead, like a forbidden thing becoming more tempting once forbidden.

insights.title: You shall not covet
insights.body: Paul uses the tenth commandment as his example (7:7). Coveting is an inward sin no one else can see; it exposed Paul's heart in a way outward obedience never could.

insights.title: The struggle
insights.body: What I want to do, I don't do; what I hate, I do (7:15). Readers have debated for centuries whether Paul describes his life before Christ, a believer's ongoing struggle, or Israel under the law. Many Christians recognize themselves either way.

insights.title: Wretched
insights.body: Paul cries, What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? (7:24). The word for wretched means worn out by hardship, someone at the end of their strength.

insights.title: Thanks be to God
insights.body: The answer is a person, not a technique: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (7:25). Chapter 8 explains how the Spirit does what the law couldn't.

insights.title: Honest about the struggle
insights.body: Paul was honest about doing what he hated. What struggle would it help to name honestly before God?

8.summary: There is no condemnation for those in Christ; the Spirit gives life, makes us God's children who cry Abba, groans with creation as it waits for freedom, and helps us pray; God works all things for good, and nothing can separate us from his love.
8.lookfor: Notice how often the Spirit is mentioned (more than in any other chapter of the letter), and the questions in the closing verses.

insights.title: No condemnation
insights.body: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). The verdict is in, and it's final. The chapter that begins with no condemnation ends with no separation.

insights.title: Adoption
insights.body: We received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (8:15). In Roman law an adopted son, often an adult, received a new name, full inheritance and a clean slate from old debts.

insights.title: Creation groans
insights.body: Creation itself groans as in childbirth, waiting to be freed from decay (8:19-22). The curse on the ground in Genesis 3 will be lifted when God's children are revealed.

insights.title: Groans too deep for words
insights.body: When we don't know how to pray, the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings that can't be uttered (8:26). Even our wordless prayers are carried.

insights.title: All things for good
insights.body: God works all things together for good for those who love him (8:28). Not that all things are good, but that he weaves them toward his purpose: to shape us into the image of his Son (8:29).

insights.title: If God is for us
insights.body: If God is for us, who can be against us? He who didn't spare his own Son, how will he not also freely give us all things? (8:31-32). The echo is of Abraham not withholding Isaac.

insights.title: Nothing can separate
insights.body: Paul lists death, life, angels, powers, things present and to come (8:38-39). What do you fear might separate you from God's love?

9.summary: Paul grieves that many of his fellow Israelites have not believed, then argues that God's word has not failed: not all descended from Israel are Israel, God is free to show mercy as he chooses, and Israel stumbled by pursuing righteousness by works instead of faith.
9.lookfor: Notice Paul's anguish at the start, the examples of Isaac and Jacob, and the stumbling stone at the end.

names.name: Isaac
names.gloss: Abraham's son of promise.

names.name: Rebekah
names.gloss: Isaac's wife, mother of twins Jacob and Esau.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: The younger twin, chosen before birth, later named Israel.

names.name: Esau
names.gloss: The older twin, ancestor of Edom.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: The king of Egypt at the exodus.

names.name: Hosea
names.gloss: A prophet who spoke of God calling a not-my-people his people.

insights.title: Great sorrow
insights.body: Paul says he could wish himself cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his people (9:3), echoing Moses' offer to be blotted out of God's book for Israel.

insights.title: Has God's word failed?
insights.body: If Israel's Messiah came and most of Israel rejected him, did God's promise fail? Chapters 9 to 11 answer: no. Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel (9:6).

insights.title: Loved and hated
insights.body: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated (9:13), quoting Malachi. In Hebrew idiom, love and hate can mean chosen and not chosen, more about calling than emotion, and it concerns the nations descended from them.

insights.title: The potter
insights.body: Does the clay talk back to the potter? (9:20-21). Paul borrows the image from Isaiah and Jeremiah, where the potter is free but also patiently reshapes a spoiled vessel.

insights.title: Not my people
insights.body: Paul quotes Hosea: I will call them my people, which were not my people (9:25). Words first about restoring rebellious Israel now include the Gentiles too.

insights.title: The stumbling stone
insights.body: Israel stumbled over the stumbling stone because it pursued righteousness as if by works, not by faith (9:32-33). Paul combines two stone passages from Isaiah.

insights.title: Grieving for others
insights.body: Paul's theology came with tears for people who didn't share his faith. Whose spiritual state do you care about that deeply?

10.summary: Paul prays for Israel's salvation, explains that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness, that the word of faith is near, and that everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, which is why messengers must be sent.
10.lookfor: Notice the chain of questions in verses 14 and 15, and how simple Paul makes the way of salvation.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The lawgiver, quoted on both law and faith.

names.name: Isaiah
names.gloss: The prophet quoted on beautiful feet and on Israel's unbelief.

insights.title: A zeal without knowledge
insights.body: Paul says Israel has a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (10:2). He speaks from experience; he had been zealous himself.

insights.title: The end of the law
insights.body: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness (10:4). The word telos can mean termination or goal; many hear both: the law's goal is reached in Christ, so it no longer serves as a route to righteousness.

insights.title: The word is near you
insights.body: Paul applies Moses' words, the word is near you, in your mouth and heart (10:8), to the message of faith. No one needs to climb to heaven to bring Christ down; he has already come.

insights.title: Confess and believe
insights.body: If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved (10:9). Whoever calls on the Lord's name will be saved (10:13), quoting Joel.

insights.title: How will they hear?
insights.body: How can they call on one they haven't believed, believe one they haven't heard, hear without a preacher, or preach unless sent? (10:14-15). Paul's mission to Spain is the backdrop.

insights.title: Beautiful feet
insights.body: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news (10:15), quoting Isaiah's picture of a runner coming over the mountains to announce victory and the return of exiles.

insights.title: Sent
insights.body: Paul asks how anyone will hear without someone to tell them. Who in your life might never hear unless you speak?

11.summary: God has not rejected Israel: a remnant believes, Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles, Gentiles grafted into the olive tree must not boast, and in the end all Israel will be saved; Paul closes with praise for God's unsearchable wisdom.
11.lookfor: Notice the olive tree illustration and its warning to Gentile believers, and the burst of praise at the end.

names.name: Elijah
names.gloss: The prophet who thought he alone was faithful.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: Paul's tribe, the smallest of Israel's tribes.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, from which the deliverer comes.

insights.title: I am an Israelite
insights.body: Has God rejected his people? May it never be! Paul himself is an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin (11:1). He is living proof of a believing remnant.

insights.title: Seven thousand
insights.body: Elijah thought he alone was left, but God had kept seven thousand who hadn't bowed to Baal (11:4). The faithful remnant is often larger than it looks.

insights.title: Stumbling to bless
insights.body: Israel's stumbling brought salvation to the Gentiles, to provoke Israel to jealousy (11:11). If their rejection meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion?

insights.title: Grafting olive trees
insights.body: Gentiles are wild olive shoots grafted into a cultivated tree (11:17). Farmers usually grafted cultivated branches into wild stock; Paul admits his picture is contrary to nature (11:24), which is the point: grace defies the usual order.

insights.title: Don't boast
insights.body: Gentile believers must not boast over the broken-off branches: you don't support the root, the root supports you (11:18). Christians have too often ignored this warning about Jewish people.

insights.title: All Israel will be saved
insights.body: A partial hardening has come on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved (11:25-26). Readers debate what all Israel means, but Paul's hope for his people is clear.

insights.title: Oh the depth
insights.body: After three chapters of hard argument, Paul ends in worship: oh the depth of the riches and wisdom of God (11:33). When did understanding something about God lead you to praise?

12.summary: In view of God's mercies, Paul urges believers to offer themselves as living sacrifices and be transformed in mind, to use their varied gifts as one body, to love sincerely, and to overcome evil with good.
12.lookfor: Notice the "therefore" that links practice to the theology of chapters 1 to 11, and the rapid-fire commands about love.

insights.title: Therefore
insights.body: Paul begins, I urge you therefore by the mercies of God (12:1). Everything in chapters 12 to 15 grows out of the mercy described in chapters 1 to 11. Grace comes first; response follows.

insights.title: A living sacrifice
insights.body: Offer your bodies as a living sacrifice (12:1), a deliberate paradox, since sacrifices died. Your reasonable service can also be translated your spiritual worship: worship is the whole of life.

insights.title: Transformed
insights.body: Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind (12:2). The word for transformed is the root of metamorphosis, used of Jesus' transfiguration.

insights.title: One body
insights.body: We are many members in one body, with different gifts (12:4-6). Paul develops the same picture more fully in 1 Corinthians.

insights.title: Coals of fire
insights.body: Feed your hungry enemy and you will heap coals of fire on his head (12:20), quoting Proverbs. Probably the burning shame that leads to repentance; some link it to an Egyptian ritual of carrying coals as a sign of remorse.

insights.title: Overcome evil with good
insights.body: Don't repay evil for evil; don't take revenge, but leave room for God's wrath (12:17-21). These commands echo Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, and would be needed under coming persecution.

insights.title: Rejoice and weep
insights.body: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep (12:15). Which is harder for you, and with whom could you practice it this week?

13.summary: Paul tells believers to submit to governing authorities as God's servants and pay taxes, to owe nothing but love, since love fulfills the law, and to wake up and put on the Lord Jesus Christ because the day is near.
13.lookfor: Notice how love sums up the commandments, and the urgency of the closing image of night and day.

insights.title: Taxes in Rome
insights.body: Paul urges paying taxes and honor to authorities (13:6-7). Around this time Romans were protesting heavy indirect taxes, and Jews had recently been expelled from the city; quiet faithfulness mattered.

insights.title: Authority from God
insights.body: There is no authority except from God (13:1). Paul writes under Nero's early, stable years. This chapter gives a general principle, not unconditional obedience: the apostles also said they must obey God rather than men.

insights.title: The debt of love
insights.body: Owe no one anything, except to love one another (13:8). Love is a debt we can never pay off.

insights.title: Love fulfills the law
insights.body: The commandments are summed up in this: love your neighbor as yourself (13:9), from Leviticus, as Jesus taught.

insights.title: The night is far gone
insights.body: It's time to wake up, for salvation is nearer than when we first believed; the night is almost over and the day is near (13:11-12). The hope of Christ's return shapes how believers live now.

insights.title: Augustine's verse
insights.body: Augustine, struggling to give up his old life, heard a child's voice say take up and read, opened to 13:13-14, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and was converted. The story is in his Confessions.

insights.title: Putting on Christ
insights.body: Paul says to put on Christ like clothing (13:14). What would it look like to put him on deliberately each morning?

14.summary: Paul addresses disputes over food and holy days: the strong and the weak must not judge or despise each other, since each serves the Lord; the strong should give up their freedom rather than cause a brother to stumble.
14.lookfor: Notice who Paul calls strong and weak, and how he treats both sides of the dispute.

insights.title: Meat and days
insights.body: Some believers ate only vegetables and kept special days; others ate everything (14:2, 14:5). In Rome this likely divided Jewish believers who kept food laws from Gentile believers who didn't, plus worries about meat from pagan temples.

insights.title: Weak in faith
insights.body: The weak in faith (14:1) are those whose consciences forbid things that faith in Christ actually allows. Paul agrees with the strong (14:14) but sides with love.

insights.title: Don't judge another's servant
insights.body: Who are you to judge another's servant? To his own master he stands or falls (14:4). Each believer answers to the Lord.

insights.title: Every knee
insights.body: We will all stand before God's judgment seat, for every knee will bow (14:10-11), from Isaiah. Paul uses the same verse of Jesus in Philippians.

insights.title: The kingdom isn't food
insights.body: God's kingdom is not eating and drinking but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (14:17). Don't destroy God's work for the sake of food.

insights.title: Whatever isn't of faith
insights.body: Whatever is not of faith is sin (14:23). Acting against your conscience is wrong, even if the act itself is allowed.

insights.title: Giving up a freedom
insights.body: Paul asks the strong to limit their freedom for the weaker believer's sake. Is there a freedom you could set aside out of love for someone?

15.summary: The strong should bear with the weak, following Christ, who didn't please himself; Jews and Gentiles should welcome each other as Christ welcomed them; Paul explains his mission so far, his plan to visit Rome on the way to Spain, and asks for prayer for his trip to Jerusalem.
15.lookfor: Notice the string of Old Testament quotes about Gentiles praising God, and the details of Paul's travel plans.

names.name: Jesse
names.gloss: David's father; the root of Jesse means the Messiah from David's line.

names.name: Illyricum
names.gloss: A Roman province along the Adriatic coast, roughly former Yugoslavia.

names.name: Spain
names.gloss: The far western edge of the known world, where Paul hoped to go.

names.name: Macedonia
names.gloss: Northern Greece, whose churches gave to the collection.

names.name: Achaia
names.gloss: Southern Greece, around Corinth.

insights.title: Christ didn't please himself
insights.body: Even Christ didn't please himself (15:3). Paul grounds the call to bear with others' weaknesses in the example of Jesus, quoting Psalm 69.

insights.title: Welcome one another
insights.body: Receive one another, as Christ also received you (15:7). This is the practical goal of the whole letter: Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome accepting each other.

insights.title: Gentiles praising God
insights.body: Paul quotes the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, all showing the nations praising Israel's God (15:9-12). The inclusion of Gentiles was in Scripture all along.

insights.title: From Jerusalem to Illyricum
insights.body: Paul has preached the gospel fully from Jerusalem around to Illyricum (15:19), an arc of over a thousand miles. He aims to preach where Christ hasn't been named.

insights.title: The collection
insights.body: Paul is taking money from Gentile churches to poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25-27). It was a sign of unity: Gentiles who shared in Israel's spiritual blessings sharing material ones.

insights.title: Pray for me
insights.body: Paul asks prayer to be rescued from unbelievers in Judea (15:30-31). Acts tells how he was arrested there, and he did reach Rome, though in chains.

insights.title: The God of hope
insights.body: Paul prays that the God of hope fill them with joy and peace (15:13). Where do you need that kind of hope right now?

16.summary: Paul commends Phoebe, who carries the letter, greets many believers in Rome by name, warns against those who cause divisions, sends greetings from his companions, and ends with praise to the God who is able to strengthen them.
16.lookfor: Notice how many women are greeted and the variety of names: Jewish, Greek, Latin, slave and free.

names.name: Phoebe
names.gloss: A servant (deacon) of the church at Cenchreae, who likely carried the letter.

names.name: Cenchreae
names.gloss: Corinth's eastern port.

names.name: Prisca
names.gloss: Priscilla, with her husband Aquila Paul's fellow workers.

names.name: Junia
names.gloss: A believer greeted with Andronicus, noted among the apostles.

names.name: Rufus
names.gloss: Possibly the son of Simon of Cyrene.

names.name: Tertius
names.gloss: The scribe who wrote the letter down.

names.name: Erastus
names.gloss: The treasurer of the city of Corinth.

skim.advice: Most of this chapter is a list of greetings; skim the names, noticing the many women and the house churches, then read verses 17 to 27.

insights.title: Phoebe
insights.body: Phoebe is a servant, or deacon, of the church and a patron of many, including Paul (16:1-2). As the likely courier, she may also have read and explained the letter to the Romans.

insights.title: Many women
insights.body: Of about 26 people greeted, around ten are women, several described as hard workers in the Lord (16:6, 16:12). Women were central to the Roman church.

insights.title: Junia among the apostles
insights.body: Andronicus and Junia, Paul's relatives, were in prison with him and are notable among the apostles (16:7). Most ancient writers read Junia as a woman's name.

insights.title: Rufus and his mother
insights.body: Mark mentions that Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus' cross, was the father of Alexander and Rufus. If this is the same Rufus (16:13), the man compelled to carry the cross had a family that followed Jesus. Paul says Rufus's mother had been a mother to him too.

insights.title: Erastus the treasurer
insights.body: Erastus, the city treasurer, sends greetings (16:23). An inscription found in Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense as a city official; he may be the same man.

insights.title: Crushing Satan
insights.body: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (16:20), echoing the promise in Genesis that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head.

insights.title: Names that matter
insights.body: Paul remembered dozens of people by name and what they'd done. Whom could you thank by name this week for how they've served?

intro.who: Paul wrote it, with Tertius as his scribe (16:22). He had not yet visited Rome.
intro.when: About AD 57, from Corinth, near the end of his third journey, just before taking a gift to Jerusalem (15:25-26).
intro.why: To set out the gospel he preached to a church he hoped to visit and enlist for a mission to Spain, and to help Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome accept each other. It is Paul's fullest explanation of how God puts people right with himself.

outline.title: Right with God by faith, like Abraham
New life in Christ and the Spirit
